newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seeks "extraordinary alertness" on North.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seeks "extraordinary alertness" on North.

text.p: South Korean Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung on Tuesday called for "extraordinary alertness" against North Korea, saying a top Pyongyang official"s defection showed serious instability in the Stalinist North.

"The defection of secretary Hwang Jang-yop, who belongs to the core force of the North Korean leadership, vividly displays the shaking of the ideological foundation that has supported the North Korean system amid economic disasters," he said.
Hwang, one of 11 powerful secretaries of the ruling Worker"s Party along with North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, has been holed up at Seoul"s mission in Beijing since last Wednesday.
Lee told parliament that the communist North had increasingly deployed offensive forces near the border with the South, despite an economic crisis and chronic food shortage.
He said the shooting of a prominent defector near Seoul at the weekend after Hwang sought political asylum in Beijing reminded the country about the importance of security.
"I think what we need at this point of time...is extraordinary alertness and realisation," Lee said, adding his government would give top priority to security on the divided Korean peninsula.
He said North Korea lacked "reasonable power to control" and could resort to "direct or indirect provocation" in the run-up to South Korea"s presidential elections in December.
Seoul has accused Pyongyang of sending agents to shoot defector Li Il-nam, a nephew of Kim Jong-il"s former wife, near Seoul in an apparent warning to South Korea and other potential asylum seekers.
Li, known in the South as Lee Hang-yong, remains in a coma.
Prime minister Lee said his country would spare no diplomatic efforts to allow Hwang, ranked 24th in Pyongyang"s hierarchy, to be granted political asylum.
The North has hinted it may accept Hwang"s defection, saying it would dismiss him if he sought asylum, Seoul officials said.
"It is certain North Korea is changing its attitude," said Kim Kyung-woong, a senior official at the state South-North Dialogue Office.
"North Korea appears to be acknowledging that things are not developing as it wants in the Hwang Jang-yop case," he said. "North Korea is widening its options."
Pyongyang had maintained that Seoul kidnapped Hwang, a claim brushed aside by Seoul as "preposterous".
Pyongyang"s Foreign Ministry, commenting on its highest level defection yet, said late on Monday that if Hwang had been kidnapped, then North Korea would take "decisive countermeasures".
"Our stand is simple and clear. If he was kidnapped, we cannot tolerate it and we will take decisive countermeasures," said a ministry statement, carried by its official media.
But the statement late on Monday added: "If he sought asylum, it means that he is a renegade and he is dismissed."
Another senior Seoul official, who asked not to be identified, said: "The statement"s wording signals that North Korea might accept Hwang"s defection."
The North Korean statement was issued after the North"s ambassador was believed to have met officials at China"s Foreign Ministry on Monday.
"I think the statement was issued after Pyongyang consulted with China," said Nam Man-kwon, a senior fellow at Seoul"s state-financed Institute of Defence Analysis.
